fetched_contents.text: Recent Progress in Long-Term Sleep Monitoring Technology Abstract Sleep is an essential physiological activity, accounting for about one-third of our lives, which significantly impacts our memory, mood, health, and children’s growth. Especially after the COVID-19 epidemic, sleep health issues have attracted more attention. In recent years, with the development of wearable electronic devices, there have been more and more studies, products, or solutions related to sleep monitoring. Many mature technologies, such as polysomnography, have been applied to clinical practice. However, it is urgent to develop wearable or non-contacting electronic devices suitable for household continuous sleep monitoring. This paper first introduces the basic knowledge of sleep and the significance of sleep monitoring. Then, according to the types of physiological signals monitored, this paper describes the research progress of bioelectrical signals, biomechanical signals, and biochemical signals used for sleep monitoring. However, it is not ideal to monitor the sleep quality for the whole night based on only one signal. Therefore, this paper reviews the research on multi-signal monitoring and introduces systematic sleep monitoring schemes. Finally, a conclusion and discussion of sleep monitoring are presented to propose potential future directions and prospects for sleep monitoring. Keywords: biosensors, sleep monitoring, polysomnography, REM sleep 1. Introduction 1.1. Sleep Sleep takes up about one-third of our lives. As shown in Figure 1, the COVID-19 outbreak has affected people’s sleep in many ways [1,2,3,4,5]. In the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak, it has been reported that many people’s sleep duration has increased, but at the same time, the sleep quality has declined, and the sleep time has changed [1]. Statistics have shown that 18.2% of people have poor sleep quality [2]. There was a general increase in the impact of sleep deficits and mental health burdens on healthcare workers. Sleep deprivation has increased prevalence in patients with acute and long-term COVID-19. Dreams under the epidemic [6] and post-vaccine effects [4] also impact sleep. We should pay more attention to how people can achieve good quality sleep, including restful sleep, no daytime sleepiness, and adequate objective sleep depth [7]. Sleep duration and quality are the core indicators to evaluate whether a person has healthy sleep. Where sleep duration is easier to measure, evaluating sleep quality needs to find an easier metric. The microstructural sleep analysis of the cyclic alternating pattern may be related to self-reported sleep quality, that is, the measurement of the total duration of sleep and the analysis of sleep cycles are normally the most important for analyzing sleep quality (this will be specified in Section 2.2) [8]. 1.2. Sleep Problems Inadequate, irregular, or poor-quality sleep is common in modern society. Factors contributing to sleep deprivation include occupation, social demands, mental illness, physical illness, sleep disorders, race, age, marital status, gender, and hospitalization [10,11]. Sleep deprivation or sleep disorders can lead to low cognition, poor alertness, poor mood, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, metabolic and immune disorders, and even death [12,13]. For particular groups, sleep problems also have their own unique manifestations. Adolescents tend to sleep late, wake up early during school days, and catch up on sleep on weekends [14], leading to differences in their sleep on weekdays and days off [14,15]. Some older adults also experience sleep disturbances because the circadian system and sleep balance mechanisms become less robust with normal aging [16]. Finally, women with severe premenstrual syndrome (PMS) have poorer sleep quality, which may be related to altered melatonin rhythms [17]. There are also a variety of sleep disorders that may affect patients’ quality of life, such as obstructive sleep apnea, chronic insomnia, narcolepsy, delayed sleep–wake phase disorder, and Kleine–Levin syndrome [3]. For people with neurological and metabolic disorders, sleep quality is critical to health and even life. A classic example is people with depression. Antidepressant medications may affect sleep structure. Persistent sleep problems can, in turn, increase depression relapse or increased drug dependence and even potentially cause suicide in patients [18,19]. Attention to sleep problems can help determine the best medication regimen for depressed patients. In addition, for pregnant women, clinical pregnancy and live birth have occurred in 35% of women with sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) compared to 58% of women without SDB [20]. Sleep impairment is also a common comorbid and debilitating symptom for persons with opioid use disorder (OUD). Research into underlying mechanisms and efficacious treatment interventions for OUD-related sleep problems requires both precise and physiologic measurements of sleep-related outcomes and impairment [21]. 1.3. Summary Sleep is a complex physiological behavior, and the physiological signals and sensing techniques associated with sleep are diverse. Sleep problems are very common in the current society. Sleep monitoring technology is also very rich. However, at present, the most accurate monitoring system is for clinical use (in Section 2.1), which is difficult to use in daily life. There is a lot of research space for the technology that allows people to detect long-term sleep at home. Introduction Sleep is critical for a wide range of physiological and cognitive functions, including memory consolidation [1], metabolic regulation [2], immune function [3], and emotional stability [4]. Disrupted or insufficient sleep has been linked to numerous adverse health outcomes, ranging from cardiovascular disease and diabetes to depression and cognitive decline [2,4,5]. The profound impact of sleep on overall well-being has driven decades of technological innovation aimed at understanding and monitoring sleep quality and architecture. Historically, polysomnography (PSG), considered the gold standard for sleep assessment, has offered comprehensive insights into sleep stages, including wakefulness, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and non-REM sleep (N1, N2, N3) [6]. PSG involves the recording of multiple physiological parameters, such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), and electrocardiography (ECG), during an overnight stay in a sleep laboratory [6]. While PSG provides rich data, its high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab limit its practicality for widespread and long-term sleep monitoring. These limitations have necessitated the development of more accessible and convenient alternatives for sleep assessment. Recent advances in wearable technology, including advancements in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization, have opened avenues for longitudinal, non-invasive sleep assessment in naturalistic settings, outside the confines of a sleep laboratory [7,8]. These devices, from wrist actigraphy to smart headbands/smartwatches, offer the potential to capture sleep-related data over extended periods, providing a more comprehensive and ecologically valid picture of an individual’s sleep patterns. This review aims to provide an in-depth narrative on the evolution, current state, and prospective future of wearable sleep monitors, exploring the various types of devices, their underlying technologies, and their accuracy in assessing sleep parameters. Practical disadvantages of PSG that affect long-term use

The main practical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring revolve around patient comfort, logistical burden, and the difficulty of repeated use. First, PSG is often uncomfortable for patients and can reduce sleep quality during setup. Evidence explicitly notes that PSG “remains uncomfortable for many patients, often requiring overnight stays in unfamiliar environments” [N2-R3], and another source states that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort is compounded by the fact that PSG is designed to obtain “maximum clinically relevant physiological information with the least disruption of the patient's normal sleep” [N2-R2], yet in practice, the setup itself can interfere with normal sleep and comfort.

Second, the time and effort needed for nightly recalibration and electrode placement make repeated use burdensome. The same evidence on PSG limitations emphasizes that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. These factors imply that each PSG session is not a simple one-time event; it requires careful electrode placement, monitoring, and interpretation, which is impractical for repeated or prolonged monitoring. The practical implication is that PSG is not well suited for long-term tracking because it demands significant staff involvement and setup time rather than being a low-maintenance, scalable solution.

Third, patients often lack tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions. The literature here points to discomfort and poor sleep quality as the primary reasons why repeated PSG use is difficult [N2-R3], and also notes that long-term compliance with PAP devices remains problematic as a separate but related issue [N2-R4]. While this last point is about PAP rather than PSG, it reinforces the broader theme that long-term monitoring is hard when the intervention itself is intrusive and uncomfortable. In other words, the repeated requirement to undergo PSG can become a burden rather than a routine part of care, reducing its feasibility for long-term use.

Overall, the practical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are not just about the equipment itself but also about the patient experience, the effort required for each session, and the difficulty of maintaining compliance over repeated or prolonged periods. These factors make PSG less suitable for continuous or extended sleep monitoring in real-world settings [N2-R3], [N1-R4], [N5-F2].

Clinical and research limitations of PSG for extended sleep assessment

PSG has important clinical and research limitations when used for extended sleep assessment, particularly in capturing longitudinal or circadian patterns reliably, detecting brief or intermittent events, and generalizing lab findings to real-world sleep. 

First, PSG is limited in its ability to capture longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably. The evidence states that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s typical sleep environment [N5-F2]. This is a key limitation for extended assessment because PSG is a snapshot of sleep under controlled conditions, not a continuous record of natural sleep behavior. The same review also notes that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], which suggests that repeated or extended PSG may not be practical enough to generate reliable longitudinal data. In addition, the cited PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring explicitly frames PSG as a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life, highlighting the gap between laboratory PSG and real-world sleep monitoring [N1-F1]. That means PSG is less suitable for studying how sleep changes over time or across circadian rhythms.

Second, PSG is sensitive to brief or intermittent events that may be missed. The evidence shows that PSG is considered the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation [N4-R3], but it also emphasizes that PSG is limited by the artificial environment of the sleep lab and the need for specialized equipment [N5-F2]. This implies that PSG can miss events that occur in the lab but not in natural settings, or events that are brief and intermittent. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise points to the need for wearable or non-contacting devices for household continuous sleep monitoring, because relying on only one signal is not ideal for whole-night monitoring [N1-F1]. This suggests that PSG’s reliance on a fixed set of electrodes and sensors may not fully capture the dynamic and variable nature of sleep, especially when events are short-lived or occur outside the typical PSG setup.

Third, PSG findings are difficult to generalize to real-world sleep. The evidence repeatedly stresses that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. The review explicitly states that the limitations of PSG include “the high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab” [N5-F2], and the PMC article similarly frames PSG as a method that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1]. This means that PSG results can be highly context-dependent and may not represent how a person sleeps at home, in other settings, or across different days. The clinical implication is that PSG findings may be less useful for understanding real-world sleep patterns, sleep disorders, or treatment outcomes when those patterns are intermittent or influenced by external factors.

In summary, PSG’s limitations for extended sleep assessment are structural: it is not designed for continuous, naturalistic, or longitudinal monitoring; it may miss brief or intermittent events; and its lab-based nature makes it hard to generalize to everyday life. These limitations are central to why alternative monitoring approaches have developed [N5-F2], [N1-F1], and why PSG is better suited to diagnosis than to long-term sleep assessment [N5-F2].

Technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring

The technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are centered on sensor burden, movement/artifact interference, and the requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff, along with limited portability and difficulty with home or ambulatory deployment.

First, PSG places a significant sensor burden on the patient, which can lead to movement and artifact interference during prolonged use. The evidence states that PSG involves simultaneous recording of multiple physiological parameters related to sleep and wakefulness [N4-R2], and that it is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise notes that PSG is a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which implies that the equipment and setup required for PSG are not compatible with prolonged or continuous monitoring outside a controlled environment. This sensor burden is especially problematic for long-term use because prolonged attachment can cause discomfort, movement artifacts, and reduced data quality over time [N2-R3], [N1-F1].

Second, PSG requires dedicated equipment and trained staff, making it less scalable for repeated or prolonged monitoring. The evidence explicitly states that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. This means that PSG is not a low-cost, low-staff solution. The same PMC article frames PSG as difficult to use in daily life, reinforcing the idea that the technical infrastructure needed for PSG is not suitable for long-term, frequent, or home-based use [N1-F1]. In addition, the home PSG literature notes that while home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], it is still constrained by the need for equipment and the challenges of deployment outside the lab [N6-R3]. This shows that the technical requirements of PSG persist even in home or ambulatory settings, limiting its practicality for long-term monitoring.

Third, PSG is limited in portability and difficult to deploy at home or ambulatory. The evidence highlights that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2], and that home PSG is “technically feasible with relatively low failure rates” [N6-R2]. However, technical feasibility does not equate to ease of home use. The home PSG literature also notes that the study included synchronous in-lab Embletta and PSG, and home Embletta [N6-R3], indicating that even portable systems are still tied to in-lab reference standards and may require careful calibration. The PMC article likewise argues that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous sleep monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. Taken together, this means that PSG’s technical limitations include limited portability, the need for specialized equipment, and the difficulty of deploying it outside the lab, all of which make long-term monitoring challenging [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

Overall, the technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are that it is sensor-heavy, prone to movement/artifact interference, requires dedicated equipment and trained staff, and is difficult to deploy at home or ambulatorily [N4-R2], [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

How alternative methods address PSG limitations

Alternative methods such as wearables and home monitoring are positioned as responses to PSG’s limitations, but they come with trade-offs in accuracy, detail, and clinical validity, and they are not a universal replacement for PSG.

First, wearables and home monitoring offer greater convenience and portability compared to PSG. The evidence states that wearable technologies enable “non-invasive, long-term, and real-world monitoring” [N5-F2], and that they are useful for longitudinal sleep assessment outside the sleep laboratory [N5-F2]. The same review notes that advances in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization have opened avenues for sleep monitoring in naturalistic settings [N5-F2]. This is a direct response to PSG’s limitation of being confined to sleep laboratories and requiring specialized equipment [N5-F2], [N1-F1]. Wearable devices also reduce the burden of repeated electrode placement and recalibration, making them more suitable for long-term use [N5-F2].

Second, these alternatives trade off accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. The evidence shows that consumer sleep-tracking devices differ significantly from PSG in their estimation of sleep stages, with some overestimating and others underestimating sleep parameters [N5-R2]. The narrative review likewise states that PSG is the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation, while wearable technologies are emerging alternatives with strengths and limitations [N5-F2]. This means that while wearables can provide useful data, they do not replace PSG’s detailed, multi-parameter, and expert-interpreted assessment. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as the most accurate clinical technique but notes that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. So the trade-off is that alternatives are more convenient and portable, but they are less detailed and less accurate than PSG.

Third, alternatives are suitable for some contexts but not all, and PSG remains necessary for specific diagnostic or research purposes. The evidence indicates that PSG remains the go-to method for diagnosing sleep disorders and providing in-depth analysis [N5-R4]. It also notes that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], and that PSG is still used for sleep disorder diagnostics [N5-F2]. This suggests that alternatives are useful for screening, longitudinal monitoring, and real-world data collection, but PSG remains necessary when precise staging, fragmentation assessment, or detailed physiological interpretation is needed. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. This reinforces that PSG is not universally replaced by alternatives; it remains the gold standard in many diagnostic and research contexts [N5-F2], [N5-R4].

In conclusion, alternative methods address PSG limitations by improving portability, convenience, and longitudinal use, but they do so at the cost of reduced accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. Wearables and home monitoring are therefore suitable for some applications, but PSG remains necessary for precise diagnosis and in-depth sleep assessment [N5-F2], [N5-R4], [N6-R2].

## Main disadvantages of polysomnography (PSG) that make it challenging for long-term sleep monitoring

Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosing sleep disorders, but it is not well suited for long-term sleep monitoring because of a combination of technical, practical, clinical, and logistical disadvantages. These limitations make PSG difficult to use repeatedly, continuously, or in real-world settings. Below is an integrated synthesis of the main disadvantages.

---

### 1) Technical disadvantages that limit long-term monitoring

The most fundamental technical problem with PSG for long-term monitoring is its sensor burden and the way it interacts with prolonged use. PSG requires simultaneous recording of multiple physiological signals, including EEG, EOG, EMG, and respiratory and cardiac signals [N4-R2], and it is described as “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. That makes it inherently cumbersome for continuous or extended monitoring. The evidence also says PSG is a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which underscores the technical mismatch between PSG’s lab-based design and the demands of long-term, home-based monitoring.

A second technical limitation is movement/artifact interference during prolonged use. PSG is uncomfortable for many patients and often requires overnight stays in unfamiliar environments [N2-R3]. The same evidence notes that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort can lead to movement, restlessness, and artifact contamination in the data, especially over time. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring also highlights that relying on only one signal is not ideal for whole-night monitoring [N1-F1], implying that PSG’s multi-sensor setup is not naturally compatible with prolonged, artifact-free monitoring.

A third technical problem is the requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff. PSG is not a low-cost, low-staff solution; it is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4], and it “requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. This makes repeated or prolonged use impractical in routine settings. Even in home or ambulatory deployment, the evidence indicates that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], but it still faces deployment challenges outside the lab [N6-R3]. So the technical burden of PSG persists even when it is moved closer to the patient.

Finally, PSG is limited in portability and difficult to deploy at home or ambulatorily. The evidence repeatedly notes that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. That means PSG is not designed for continuous, naturalistic monitoring. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. Taken together, this means PSG is not a practical solution for long-term, portable, or ambulatory monitoring [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

---

### 2) Practical disadvantages affecting long-term use

The practical disadvantages of PSG are closely tied to patient comfort, compliance, and the effort required for repeated use. First, PSG is uncomfortable for many patients and can reduce sleep quality during setup. The evidence explicitly states that PSG “remains uncomfortable for many patients, often requiring overnight stays in unfamiliar environments” [N2-R3], and that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort is a major barrier to repeated or prolonged monitoring because it can disrupt the sleep process itself.

Second, nightly recalibration and electrode placement are time-consuming and effort-intensive. The evidence states that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. These factors imply that each PSG session is not a simple one-time event; it requires careful setup, monitoring, and interpretation. For long-term use, that means PSG is not scalable or efficient enough to support frequent or extended monitoring.

Third, patients often lack tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions. The literature here emphasizes discomfort and poor sleep quality as the primary reasons why repeated PSG use is difficult [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that long-term compliance with PAP devices remains problematic [N2-R4], which reinforces the broader theme that long-term monitoring is hard when the intervention itself is intrusive and uncomfortable. In other words, the repeated requirement to undergo PSG can become a burden rather than a routine part of care, reducing its feasibility for long-term use.

---

### 3) Clinical and research limitations for extended sleep assessment

PSG’s limitations are especially important when used for extended sleep assessment. One major limitation is that PSG is poor at capturing longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably. The evidence states that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s typical sleep environment [N5-F2]. This means PSG provides a snapshot of sleep under controlled conditions rather than a continuous record of natural sleep behavior. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which highlights the gap between laboratory PSG and real-world monitoring.

Second, PSG is sensitive to brief or intermittent events that may be missed. PSG is considered the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation [N4-R3], but it is also limited by the artificial environment of the sleep lab and the need for specialized equipment [N5-F2]. This implies that PSG can miss events that occur in the lab but not in natural settings, or events that are brief and intermittent. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring also points to the need for wearable or non-contacting devices for household continuous sleep monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. This suggests that PSG’s reliance on a fixed set of electrodes and sensors may not fully capture the dynamic and variable nature of sleep.

Third, PSG findings are difficult to generalize to real-world sleep. The evidence repeatedly stresses that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. The same review notes that PSG is limited by the high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab [N5-F2]. This means PSG results can be highly context-dependent and may not represent how a person sleeps at home, in other settings, or across different days. The clinical implication is that PSG findings may be less useful for understanding real-world sleep patterns, sleep disorders, or treatment outcomes when those patterns are intermittent or influenced by external factors.

---

### 4) How alternative methods address PSG limitations

Alternative methods such as wearables and home monitoring are positioned as responses to PSG’s limitations, but they come with trade-offs in accuracy, detail, and clinical validity. Wearable technologies enable “non-invasive, long-term, and real-world monitoring” [N5-F2], and advances in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization have opened avenues for sleep monitoring in naturalistic settings [N5-F2]. This directly addresses PSG’s limitation of being confined to sleep laboratories and requiring specialized equipment [N5-F2], [N1-F1]. Wearable devices also reduce the burden of repeated electrode placement and recalibration, making them more suitable for long-term use [N5-F2].

However, these alternatives trade off accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. The evidence shows that consumer sleep-tracking devices differ significantly from PSG in their estimation of sleep stages, with some overestimating and others underestimating sleep parameters [N5-R2]. The narrative review likewise states that PSG is the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation, while wearable technologies are emerging alternatives with strengths and limitations [N5-F2]. This means that while wearables can provide useful data, they do not replace PSG’s detailed, multi-parameter, and expert-interpreted assessment. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as the most accurate clinical technique but notes that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. So the trade-off is convenience and portability versus reduced accuracy and detail.

Alternatives are also not a universal replacement for PSG. The evidence indicates that PSG remains the go-to method for diagnosing sleep disorders and providing in-depth analysis [N5-R4]. It also notes that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], and that PSG is still used for sleep disorder diagnostics [N5-F2]. This suggests that alternatives are useful for screening, longitudinal monitoring, and real-world data collection, but PSG remains necessary when precise staging, fragmentation assessment, or detailed physiological interpretation is needed. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. This reinforces that PSG is not universally replaced by alternatives; it remains the gold standard in many diagnostic and research contexts [N5-F2], [N5-R4].

---

### Bottom line

The main disadvantages of PSG that make it challenging for long-term sleep monitoring are:

- **Sensor burden and movement/artifact interference** during prolonged use [N4-R2], [N5-F2], [N1-F1],  
- **Requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff** [N5-F2], [N1-R4],  
- **Limited portability and difficulty with home or ambulatory deployment** [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2],  
- **Patient discomfort and poor sleep quality during setup** [N2-R3], [N1-F1],  
- **Time and effort needed for nightly recalibration and electrode placement** [N5-F2], [N1-R4],  
- **Lack of tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions** [N2-R3], [N2-R4],  
- **Inability to capture longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably** [N5-F2], [N1-F1],  
- **Sensitivity to brief or intermittent events that may be missed** [N4-R3], [N5-F2],  
- **Difficulty generalizing lab PSG findings to real-world sleep** [N5-F2], [N1-F1].

In other words, PSG is excellent for diagnosis, but it is not well suited for long-term, continuous, or real-world sleep monitoring because of its technical complexity, patient burden, and lab-centric design [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

Practical disadvantages of PSG that affect long-term use

The main practical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring revolve around patient comfort, logistical burden, and the difficulty of repeated use. First, PSG is often uncomfortable for patients and can reduce sleep quality during setup. Evidence explicitly notes that PSG “remains uncomfortable for many patients, often requiring overnight stays in unfamiliar environments” [N2-R3], and another source states that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort is compounded by the fact that PSG is designed to obtain “maximum clinically relevant physiological information with the least disruption of the patient's normal sleep” [N2-R2], yet in practice, the setup itself can interfere with normal sleep and comfort.

Second, the time and effort needed for nightly recalibration and electrode placement make repeated use burdensome. The same evidence on PSG limitations emphasizes that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. These factors imply that each PSG session is not a simple one-time event; it requires careful electrode placement, monitoring, and interpretation, which is impractical for repeated or prolonged monitoring. The practical implication is that PSG is not well suited for long-term tracking because it demands significant staff involvement and setup time rather than being a low-maintenance, scalable solution.

Third, patients often lack tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions. The literature here points to discomfort and poor sleep quality as the primary reasons why repeated PSG use is difficult [N2-R3], and also notes that long-term compliance with PAP devices remains problematic as a separate but related issue [N2-R4]. While this last point is about PAP rather than PSG, it reinforces the broader theme that long-term monitoring is hard when the intervention itself is intrusive and uncomfortable. In other words, the repeated requirement to undergo PSG can become a burden rather than a routine part of care, reducing its feasibility for long-term use.

Overall, the practical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are not just about the equipment itself but also about the patient experience, the effort required for each session, and the difficulty of maintaining compliance over repeated or prolonged periods. These factors make PSG less suitable for continuous or extended sleep monitoring in real-world settings [N2-R3], [N1-R4], [N5-F2].

Clinical and research limitations of PSG for extended sleep assessment

PSG has important clinical and research limitations when used for extended sleep assessment, particularly in capturing longitudinal or circadian patterns reliably, detecting brief or intermittent events, and generalizing lab findings to real-world sleep. 

First, PSG is limited in its ability to capture longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably. The evidence states that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s typical sleep environment [N5-F2]. This is a key limitation for extended assessment because PSG is a snapshot of sleep under controlled conditions, not a continuous record of natural sleep behavior. The same review also notes that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], which suggests that repeated or extended PSG may not be practical enough to generate reliable longitudinal data. In addition, the cited PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring explicitly frames PSG as a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life, highlighting the gap between laboratory PSG and real-world sleep monitoring [N1-F1]. That means PSG is less suitable for studying how sleep changes over time or across circadian rhythms.

Second, PSG is sensitive to brief or intermittent events that may be missed. The evidence shows that PSG is considered the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation [N4-R3], but it also emphasizes that PSG is limited by the artificial environment of the sleep lab and the need for specialized equipment [N5-F2]. This implies that PSG can miss events that occur in the lab but not in natural settings, or events that are brief and intermittent. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise points to the need for wearable or non-contacting devices for household continuous sleep monitoring, because relying on only one signal is not ideal for whole-night monitoring [N1-F1]. This suggests that PSG’s reliance on a fixed set of electrodes and sensors may not fully capture the dynamic and variable nature of sleep, especially when events are short-lived or occur outside the typical PSG setup.

Third, PSG findings are difficult to generalize to real-world sleep. The evidence repeatedly stresses that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. The review explicitly states that the limitations of PSG include “the high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab” [N5-F2], and the PMC article similarly frames PSG as a method that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1]. This means that PSG results can be highly context-dependent and may not represent how a person sleeps at home, in other settings, or across different days. The clinical implication is that PSG findings may be less useful for understanding real-world sleep patterns, sleep disorders, or treatment outcomes when those patterns are intermittent or influenced by external factors.

In summary, PSG’s limitations for extended sleep assessment are structural: it is not designed for continuous, naturalistic, or longitudinal monitoring; it may miss brief or intermittent events; and its lab-based nature makes it hard to generalize to everyday life. These limitations are central to why alternative monitoring approaches have developed [N5-F2], [N1-F1], and why PSG is better suited to diagnosis than to long-term sleep assessment [N5-F2].

Technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring

The technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are centered on sensor burden, movement/artifact interference, and the requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff, along with limited portability and difficulty with home or ambulatory deployment.

First, PSG places a significant sensor burden on the patient, which can lead to movement and artifact interference during prolonged use. The evidence states that PSG involves simultaneous recording of multiple physiological parameters related to sleep and wakefulness [N4-R2], and that it is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise notes that PSG is a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which implies that the equipment and setup required for PSG are not compatible with prolonged or continuous monitoring outside a controlled environment. This sensor burden is especially problematic for long-term use because prolonged attachment can cause discomfort, movement artifacts, and reduced data quality over time [N2-R3], [N1-F1].

Second, PSG requires dedicated equipment and trained staff, making it less scalable for repeated or prolonged monitoring. The evidence explicitly states that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. This means that PSG is not a low-cost, low-staff solution. The same PMC article frames PSG as difficult to use in daily life, reinforcing the idea that the technical infrastructure needed for PSG is not suitable for long-term, frequent, or home-based use [N1-F1]. In addition, the home PSG literature notes that while home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], it is still constrained by the need for equipment and the challenges of deployment outside the lab [N6-R3]. This shows that the technical requirements of PSG persist even in home or ambulatory settings, limiting its practicality for long-term monitoring.

Third, PSG is limited in portability and difficult to deploy at home or ambulatory. The evidence highlights that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2], and that home PSG is “technically feasible with relatively low failure rates” [N6-R2]. However, technical feasibility does not equate to ease of home use. The home PSG literature also notes that the study included synchronous in-lab Embletta and PSG, and home Embletta [N6-R3], indicating that even portable systems are still tied to in-lab reference standards and may require careful calibration. The PMC article likewise argues that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous sleep monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. Taken together, this means that PSG’s technical limitations include limited portability, the need for specialized equipment, and the difficulty of deploying it outside the lab, all of which make long-term monitoring challenging [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

Overall, the technical disadvantages of PSG for long-term monitoring are that it is sensor-heavy, prone to movement/artifact interference, requires dedicated equipment and trained staff, and is difficult to deploy at home or ambulatorily [N4-R2], [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

How alternative methods address PSG limitations

Alternative methods such as wearables and home monitoring are positioned as responses to PSG’s limitations, but they come with trade-offs in accuracy, detail, and clinical validity, and they are not a universal replacement for PSG.

First, wearables and home monitoring offer greater convenience and portability compared to PSG. The evidence states that wearable technologies enable “non-invasive, long-term, and real-world monitoring” [N5-F2], and that they are useful for longitudinal sleep assessment outside the sleep laboratory [N5-F2]. The same review notes that advances in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization have opened avenues for sleep monitoring in naturalistic settings [N5-F2]. This is a direct response to PSG’s limitation of being confined to sleep laboratories and requiring specialized equipment [N5-F2], [N1-F1]. Wearable devices also reduce the burden of repeated electrode placement and recalibration, making them more suitable for long-term use [N5-F2].

Second, these alternatives trade off accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. The evidence shows that consumer sleep-tracking devices differ significantly from PSG in their estimation of sleep stages, with some overestimating and others underestimating sleep parameters [N5-R2]. The narrative review likewise states that PSG is the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation, while wearable technologies are emerging alternatives with strengths and limitations [N5-F2]. This means that while wearables can provide useful data, they do not replace PSG’s detailed, multi-parameter, and expert-interpreted assessment. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as the most accurate clinical technique but notes that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. So the trade-off is that alternatives are more convenient and portable, but they are less detailed and less accurate than PSG.

Third, alternatives are suitable for some contexts but not all, and PSG remains necessary for specific diagnostic or research purposes. The evidence indicates that PSG remains the go-to method for diagnosing sleep disorders and providing in-depth analysis [N5-R4]. It also notes that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], and that PSG is still used for sleep disorder diagnostics [N5-F2]. This suggests that alternatives are useful for screening, longitudinal monitoring, and real-world data collection, but PSG remains necessary when precise staging, fragmentation assessment, or detailed physiological interpretation is needed. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. This reinforces that PSG is not universally replaced by alternatives; it remains the gold standard in many diagnostic and research contexts [N5-F2], [N5-R4].

In conclusion, alternative methods address PSG limitations by improving portability, convenience, and longitudinal use, but they do so at the cost of reduced accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. Wearables and home monitoring are therefore suitable for some applications, but PSG remains necessary for precise diagnosis and in-depth sleep assessment [N5-F2], [N5-R4], [N6-R2].

## Main disadvantages of polysomnography (PSG) that make it challenging for long-term sleep monitoring

Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosing sleep disorders, but it is not well suited for long-term sleep monitoring because of a combination of technical, practical, clinical, and logistical disadvantages. These limitations make PSG difficult to use repeatedly, continuously, or in real-world settings. Below is an integrated synthesis of the main disadvantages.

---

### 1) Technical disadvantages that limit long-term monitoring

The most fundamental technical problem with PSG for long-term monitoring is its sensor burden and the way it interacts with prolonged use. PSG requires simultaneous recording of multiple physiological signals, including EEG, EOG, EMG, and respiratory and cardiac signals [N4-R2], and it is described as “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. That makes it inherently cumbersome for continuous or extended monitoring. The evidence also says PSG is a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which underscores the technical mismatch between PSG’s lab-based design and the demands of long-term, home-based monitoring.

A second technical limitation is movement/artifact interference during prolonged use. PSG is uncomfortable for many patients and often requires overnight stays in unfamiliar environments [N2-R3]. The same evidence notes that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort can lead to movement, restlessness, and artifact contamination in the data, especially over time. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring also highlights that relying on only one signal is not ideal for whole-night monitoring [N1-F1], implying that PSG’s multi-sensor setup is not naturally compatible with prolonged, artifact-free monitoring.

A third technical problem is the requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff. PSG is not a low-cost, low-staff solution; it is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4], and it “requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2]. This makes repeated or prolonged use impractical in routine settings. Even in home or ambulatory deployment, the evidence indicates that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], but it still faces deployment challenges outside the lab [N6-R3]. So the technical burden of PSG persists even when it is moved closer to the patient.

Finally, PSG is limited in portability and difficult to deploy at home or ambulatorily. The evidence repeatedly notes that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. That means PSG is not designed for continuous, naturalistic monitoring. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. Taken together, this means PSG is not a practical solution for long-term, portable, or ambulatory monitoring [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].

---

### 2) Practical disadvantages affecting long-term use

The practical disadvantages of PSG are closely tied to patient comfort, compliance, and the effort required for repeated use. First, PSG is uncomfortable for many patients and can reduce sleep quality during setup. The evidence explicitly states that PSG “remains uncomfortable for many patients, often requiring overnight stays in unfamiliar environments” [N2-R3], and that the most common challenge is adjusting to sleeping with monitoring equipment attached to the body [N1-F1]. This discomfort is a major barrier to repeated or prolonged monitoring because it can disrupt the sleep process itself.

Second, nightly recalibration and electrode placement are time-consuming and effort-intensive. The evidence states that PSG is “resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation” [N5-F2], and that in-lab PSG is “expensive, inconvenient for patients, time and resource intensive” [N1-R4]. These factors imply that each PSG session is not a simple one-time event; it requires careful setup, monitoring, and interpretation. For long-term use, that means PSG is not scalable or efficient enough to support frequent or extended monitoring.

Third, patients often lack tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions. The literature here emphasizes discomfort and poor sleep quality as the primary reasons why repeated PSG use is difficult [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that long-term compliance with PAP devices remains problematic [N2-R4], which reinforces the broader theme that long-term monitoring is hard when the intervention itself is intrusive and uncomfortable. In other words, the repeated requirement to undergo PSG can become a burden rather than a routine part of care, reducing its feasibility for long-term use.

---

### 3) Clinical and research limitations for extended sleep assessment

PSG’s limitations are especially important when used for extended sleep assessment. One major limitation is that PSG is poor at capturing longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably. The evidence states that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s typical sleep environment [N5-F2]. This means PSG provides a snapshot of sleep under controlled conditions rather than a continuous record of natural sleep behavior. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as a mature clinical technique that is difficult to use in daily life [N1-F1], which highlights the gap between laboratory PSG and real-world monitoring.

Second, PSG is sensitive to brief or intermittent events that may be missed. PSG is considered the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation [N4-R3], but it is also limited by the artificial environment of the sleep lab and the need for specialized equipment [N5-F2]. This implies that PSG can miss events that occur in the lab but not in natural settings, or events that are brief and intermittent. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring also points to the need for wearable or non-contacting devices for household continuous sleep monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. This suggests that PSG’s reliance on a fixed set of electrodes and sensors may not fully capture the dynamic and variable nature of sleep.

Third, PSG findings are difficult to generalize to real-world sleep. The evidence repeatedly stresses that PSG is conducted in sleep laboratories, which may not reflect an individual’s usual sleep environment [N5-F2]. The same review notes that PSG is limited by the high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab [N5-F2]. This means PSG results can be highly context-dependent and may not represent how a person sleeps at home, in other settings, or across different days. The clinical implication is that PSG findings may be less useful for understanding real-world sleep patterns, sleep disorders, or treatment outcomes when those patterns are intermittent or influenced by external factors.

---

### 4) How alternative methods address PSG limitations

Alternative methods such as wearables and home monitoring are positioned as responses to PSG’s limitations, but they come with trade-offs in accuracy, detail, and clinical validity. Wearable technologies enable “non-invasive, long-term, and real-world monitoring” [N5-F2], and advances in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization have opened avenues for sleep monitoring in naturalistic settings [N5-F2]. This directly addresses PSG’s limitation of being confined to sleep laboratories and requiring specialized equipment [N5-F2], [N1-F1]. Wearable devices also reduce the burden of repeated electrode placement and recalibration, making them more suitable for long-term use [N5-F2].

However, these alternatives trade off accuracy, detail, and clinical validity compared to PSG. The evidence shows that consumer sleep-tracking devices differ significantly from PSG in their estimation of sleep stages, with some overestimating and others underestimating sleep parameters [N5-R2]. The narrative review likewise states that PSG is the gold standard for quantifying sleep time, differentiating sleep stages, and assessing sleep fragmentation, while wearable technologies are emerging alternatives with strengths and limitations [N5-F2]. This means that while wearables can provide useful data, they do not replace PSG’s detailed, multi-parameter, and expert-interpreted assessment. The PMC article on long-term sleep monitoring likewise frames PSG as the most accurate clinical technique but notes that wearable or non-contacting devices are needed for household continuous monitoring because relying on only one signal is not ideal [N1-F1]. So the trade-off is convenience and portability versus reduced accuracy and detail.

Alternatives are also not a universal replacement for PSG. The evidence indicates that PSG remains the go-to method for diagnosing sleep disorders and providing in-depth analysis [N5-R4]. It also notes that home PSG is technically feasible with relatively low failure rates [N6-R2], and that PSG is still used for sleep disorder diagnostics [N5-F2]. This suggests that alternatives are useful for screening, longitudinal monitoring, and real-world data collection, but PSG remains necessary when precise staging, fragmentation assessment, or detailed physiological interpretation is needed. The home PSG literature also shows that ambulatory PSG is still limited by a lack of evidence in some settings, such as children [N6-R1], and that agreement between PSG and ambulatory studies has been studied but remains imperfect [N6-R4]. This reinforces that PSG is not universally replaced by alternatives; it remains the gold standard in many diagnostic and research contexts [N5-F2], [N5-R4].

---

### Bottom line

The main disadvantages of PSG that make it challenging for long-term sleep monitoring are:

- **Sensor burden and movement/artifact interference** during prolonged use [N4-R2], [N5-F2], [N1-F1],  
- **Requirement for dedicated equipment and trained staff** [N5-F2], [N1-R4],  
- **Limited portability and difficulty with home or ambulatory deployment** [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2],  
- **Patient discomfort and poor sleep quality during setup** [N2-R3], [N1-F1],  
- **Time and effort needed for nightly recalibration and electrode placement** [N5-F2], [N1-R4],  
- **Lack of tolerance for repeated or prolonged monitoring sessions** [N2-R3], [N2-R4],  
- **Inability to capture longitudinal or circadian sleep patterns reliably** [N5-F2], [N1-F1],  
- **Sensitivity to brief or intermittent events that may be missed** [N4-R3], [N5-F2],  
- **Difficulty generalizing lab PSG findings to real-world sleep** [N5-F2], [N1-F1].

In other words, PSG is excellent for diagnosis, but it is not well suited for long-term, continuous, or real-world sleep monitoring because of its technical complexity, patient burden, and lab-centric design [N5-F2], [N1-F1], [N6-R2].
